Name: Foam Sclerotherapy
Department Details:
Treatment Brief

‍

‍

What is foam sclerotherapy?

If we’re treating large varicose veins, we’ll use ultrasound guidance during your procedure. This isn’t usually necessary for smaller veins that are close to the surface, as visual guidance is sufficient.

Due to the series of tiny injections involved in the foam sclerotherapy procedure, some patients find them uncomfortable or mildly painful. The procedure usually takes around 30-45 minutes.

‍

‍

‍

Post-Procedure

Following your treatment, your nurse will help you put on a compression stocking, which you need to wear for 7 days after your procedure. You’ll wear two of these if you have both legs treated. Your nurse will explain how to wear these and bathe in them. They’ll also provide you with aftercare advice, including any post-treatment symptoms to be aware of.

You’re encouraged to go for a walk for at least 10 minutes prior to returning home.

‍

‍

‍

‍

What happens after treatment?

You should keep the compression pads, bandage, and stocking on continuously for 5 days. After this you may remove the pads and bandage and then replace the stocking which should be worn for a further 7 days. During this 7 day period, you may remove the stocking to shower and you may remove it at night if you wish. If you find the stocking comfortable and wish to wear it for longer, this may be helpful. Please bring your stocking back with you to your next visit as it may be possible to reuse it if you have further injections.

You should do plenty of walking and may generally do most normal activities without any problem. If in doubt ask your doctor.

You can be active as usual after the treatment and do not need to avoid anything in particular. However you should not drive on the day the procedure is performed, just in case you experience any visual disturbances (see below).

Name: Genicular Artery Embolization
Department Details:
Genicular artery embolization (GAE) is a minimally invasive, image-guided procedure that may be considered for selected patients with chronic knee pain related to osteoarthritis. It is not a treatment for every type of knee pain. A clinical assessment is needed to confirm the likely cause of symptoms, review previous care and decide whether GAE or another approach is appropriate. For a broader diagnosis-first overview, see our knee pain treatment guide.

What Is Genicular Artery Embolization?

The genicular arteries are small blood vessels that supply tissues around the knee. In some people with knee osteoarthritis, inflammation of the synovium, the lining of the joint, may be associated with increased small-vessel blood flow. This vascular change may contribute to ongoing inflammatory pain, but it does not explain every symptom or every cause of knee pain.

GAE uses selective embolization to reduce abnormal blood flow associated with inflamed synovial tissue. The aim is to reduce an inflammatory pain pathway while preserving the main circulation around the knee. The procedure does not remove arthritis or repair damaged cartilage.

Who May Be Evaluated for GAE?

Evaluation may be considered when knee pain is persistent, osteoarthritis is thought to be the main diagnosis and appropriate conservative treatment has not provided enough improvement. Previous care may include activity modification, physiotherapy, strengthening, weight management where relevant, medicines or selected injections.

Symptoms, examination findings, imaging, general health and treatment goals are reviewed together. GAE is not suitable for everyone, and an X-ray grade alone does not determine suitability. Our article about when knee pain may warrant a GAE assessment explains why symptom severity and daily function also matter.

How Is GAE Evaluated?

The assessment usually starts with a medical history and physical examination. The clinician may ask when the pain began, where it is felt, what activities aggravate it, whether swelling or stiffness occurs and how symptoms affect walking, sleep and daily tasks. Previous medicines, physiotherapy, injections and operations are also reviewed.

Weight-bearing X-rays are often useful when osteoarthritis is suspected. MRI or other imaging may be requested when the clinical question requires it, but it is not automatically needed for every patient. Evaluation may also consider other causes of pain, including ligament or meniscus injury, inflammatory arthritis, referred pain, infection or another structural problem.

How Is the Procedure Performed?

GAE is performed using imaging guidance. After local preparation and anaesthesia, a small catheter is introduced through an artery, commonly at the wrist or groin depending on clinical circumstances. The interventional radiologist guides the catheter into relevant genicular vessels and uses angiographic imaging to assess the blood supply.

Where abnormal vascularity is identified and treatment is appropriate, controlled embolization is performed through selected small vessels. The catheter is then removed and the access site is monitored. The exact technique, access route and embolic material depend on the patient's anatomy and the treating team's clinical judgment.

What GAE Does Not Do

  • GAE does not regrow cartilage or reverse osteoarthritis.
  • It does not correct severe deformity, major malalignment or mechanical instability.
  • It does not repair every meniscus, ligament or tendon problem.
  • It does not replace knee replacement for every patient.
  • It does not guarantee pain relief, and treatment response varies.

These limitations are why diagnosis and patient selection are central to the decision. If another condition is driving the symptoms, treatment should address that condition rather than assuming GAE will help.

Recovery and Follow-Up

Many GAE procedures are performed on a day-care basis, depending on the patient's health, access site and clinical circumstances. The team provides individualized guidance about wound care, medicines, movement and return to activity. Some temporary discomfort, bruising or skin changes may occur, and patients should follow instructions about symptoms that need medical review.

Follow-up helps assess the access site, symptoms and function. Improvement, when it occurs, may vary in timing and degree. Activity progression should be individualized rather than based on a fixed recovery promise. Read more about exercise and activity after GAE.

GAE Compared With Other Knee Pain Treatments

Knee osteoarthritis care may include education, physiotherapy, strengthening, suitable medicines, weight management, walking aids, injections, platelet-rich plasma in appropriate circumstances, surgery or GAE for selected patients. These approaches address different clinical needs, and no single option is better for every person.

GAE may be discussed when osteoarthritis-related pain persists and the evaluation suggests an inflammatory vascular target. Surgery may still be more appropriate for severe deformity, instability or advanced structural problems that require mechanical correction. Our GAE and knee replacement comparison outlines questions to discuss with the treating team.

When GAE May Not Be Appropriate

GAE may not be appropriate when pain is primarily caused by another diagnosis, when a major structural problem requires a different approach, or when infection or another urgent condition is suspected. Unsuitable vascular anatomy, impaired circulation, kidney problems, allergy considerations, bleeding risk, medicines or other health issues may also affect planning.

The decision must be individualized after evaluation. In some cases, further investigation, conservative management, a different image-guided treatment or a surgical opinion may be the safer or more relevant next step.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is GAE surgery?

GAE is a catheter-based, image-guided procedure rather than open knee surgery. It still requires medical assessment, informed consent, sterile technique and post-procedure monitoring.

Does GAE replace knee replacement?

No. GAE may be considered for selected patients, but it does not correct severe deformity or replace joint reconstruction when knee replacement is clinically indicated.

Can GAE regrow cartilage?

No. GAE aims to reduce abnormal inflammatory blood flow in selected cases. It does not regenerate cartilage or reverse structural osteoarthritis.

How do doctors decide whether GAE is suitable?

Doctors consider the diagnosis, symptom pattern, examination, imaging, previous treatment, vascular anatomy, general health and the patient's goals. Suitability cannot be decided from one symptom or scan alone.

Is MRI always needed before GAE?

No. X-rays may be sufficient for some osteoarthritis assessments. MRI or other tests may be used when the history or examination raises a question that needs further evaluation.

Can older adults be considered for GAE?

Age alone does not determine suitability. Overall health, diagnosis, function, circulation, medicines and treatment goals are more relevant. Read about the assessment of GAE for older adults.

Name: Hemorrhoidal Artery Embolization (HAE)
Department Details:
What Is Hemorrhoidal Artery Embolization?

Hemorrhoidal Artery Embolization (HAE), also called rectal artery embolization, is an image-guided procedure that aims to reduce blood flow to internal hemorrhoidal tissue. It may be discussed for selected patients with troublesome hemorrhoidal bleeding after evaluation. It is not appropriate for every patient or every cause of rectal bleeding.

For the broader picture, read about piles symptoms, assessment and treatment options.

Evaluation and Suitability

Before considering HAE, clinicians review symptoms, the pattern of bleeding, examination and any tests, previous treatments, medical history and medicines. Other causes of rectal bleeding need appropriate assessment. A colorectal or other relevant specialist may be involved in diagnosis and treatment planning.

Suitability varies with the type of hemorrhoids, predominant symptoms, arterial anatomy, general health and treatment goals. HAE may not address all symptoms, particularly significant prolapse or symptoms caused by external hemorrhoids. It is not a substitute for urgent care for heavy acute bleeding.

How Is HAE Performed?

An interventional radiologist uses imaging to guide a small catheter through an artery toward vessels supplying the hemorrhoidal tissue. Embolic materials are placed in selected arteries to reduce blood flow. Anaesthesia or sedation, procedure details and observation arrangements depend on the patient and clinical team.

Evidence, Risks and Limitations

Evidence on HAE is still developing, and long-term effectiveness and patient selection remain uncertain. The UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) considers evidence on superior rectal artery embolization inadequate and recommends its use only in research in the UK. Practice and regulatory requirements may differ by location. Discuss the evidence and alternatives with your clinician.

Possible risks include bleeding or bruising at the access site, infection, pain, reactions to contrast or effects on kidney function. Rare serious complications can include reduced blood supply to unintended tissue. Bleeding or symptoms may persist or return, and further treatment may be needed. Outcomes vary.

Alternatives and Follow-Up

Depending on diagnosis and severity, alternatives can include fibre and bowel-habit changes, medicines, office-based treatments such as banding or sclerotherapy, and surgery when appropriate. The treating clinician can explain the benefits and limitations of each option.

After HAE, follow the team’s advice about access-site care, activity, medication and follow-up. Contact the treating team promptly about worsening pain, fever, significant bleeding or other concerning symptoms. Recovery and follow-up vary by patient.

Musculoskeletal (MSK) conditions such as osteoarthritis, tendinopathy, and enthesopathy affect 1 in 4 adults, resulting in pain, loss of function and reduced quality of life. The secondary co-morbidities associated with these conditions include diabetes, obesity, and depression. Name: Prostate Artery Embolization
Department Details:
What Is Prostatic Artery Embolization?

Prostatic Artery Embolization (PAE), also called prostate artery embolization, is an image-guided procedure that may be considered for selected patients with urinary symptoms caused by benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Its goal is to reduce blood supply to prostate tissue and potentially improve symptoms over time; response varies.

Urinary symptoms have several possible causes. Read about enlarged prostate symptoms, evaluation and treatment options.

Assessment Before PAE

Clinical assessment considers symptom severity, medical and medication history, previous treatments and the effect on daily life. Tests may include urine testing, symptom scores, prostate imaging, urine-flow or bladder-emptying measurements, and other investigations when appropriate. A PSA test may be discussed when indicated.

Urology and interventional radiology teams consider whether symptoms are attributable to BPH and whether the prostate and arterial anatomy are suitable. Infection, kidney function, contrast allergy, bleeding risks, vascular disease, possible cancer and other causes of urinary symptoms may alter the plan.

How Does PAE Work?

An interventional radiologist uses imaging to guide a small catheter through an artery toward the arteries supplying the prostate. Small embolic particles are delivered to selected vessels to reduce blood flow. The approach and treatment of each side depend on arterial anatomy and the clinical assessment.

Possible Benefits, Limits and Risks

For selected patients PAE may improve urinary symptoms, but improvement is not guaranteed and may take time. Symptoms can persist or return, and additional treatment may be needed. PAE may not be suitable when another condition is the main cause of symptoms.

Possible risks include bruising or bleeding at the access site, infection, temporary pelvic discomfort or urinary symptoms, and urinary retention. Contrast reactions, effects on kidney function and unintended embolization of other tissue are also considerations. Sexual and ejaculation outcomes vary and cannot be guaranteed.

Alternatives to PAE

Management may include observation and lifestyle changes, medicines, or urologic procedures and surgery such as TURP, depending on symptoms and clinical findings. These options have different benefits and risks; no single treatment is right for everyone.

Recovery and Follow-Up

Hospital observation, return to activities and follow-up vary with the individual and procedure. Follow the treating team’s advice about access-site care, medicines and review. Seek urgent help if unable to pass urine, or for severe pain, fever, heavy bleeding or other concerning symptoms as advised by the team.

Name: Radiofrequency Ablation
Department Details:
Radiofrequency Ablation for Varicose Veins

Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is a catheter-based treatment that uses heat to close a selected superficial vein affected by reflux. It may be considered for appropriate patients after evaluation; not every visible vein requires a procedure. Read the varicose veins assessment and treatment overview.

Evaluation and Suitability

A clinician reviews symptoms, medical history and the affected veins. Duplex ultrasound may be used to map blood flow and reflux. Treatment depends on symptoms, vein anatomy, ultrasound findings, overall health and patient preferences.

How RFA Works

Under ultrasound guidance, a clinician introduces a thin catheter into the selected vein through a small access point. Radiofrequency energy heats the vein wall to close it. The treatment plan, anaesthesia and any additional procedures depend on the individual.

Risks, Limitations and Alternatives

Possible effects include bruising, discomfort, skin changes, inflammation or nerve irritation. Blood clots and other complications can occur. Some veins or symptoms may remain or return, and further treatment may be needed. The clinical team should explain benefits and risks before treatment.

Alternatives may include conservative care, endovenous laser treatment, VenaSeal adhesive closure, foam sclerotherapy or surgery, depending on the diagnosis and vein anatomy. Laser and RFA both use heat, while adhesive closure is non-thermal; suitability varies.

Recovery and Follow-Up

Walking, activity, compression stockings and follow-up recommendations vary by procedure and patient. Follow the treating team’s instructions and report new or worsening symptoms promptly.

The procedure is non-thermal and may require less local anaesthetic than some heat-based techniques, but suitability, aftercare and possible risks vary by patient.

Another advantage of VenaSeal is that it accomplishes vein closure in a non-thermal way. Medical-grade adhesive is delivered in small increments along the length of the vein followed by brief compression of the vein, not unlike sealing a small straw with super glue. Because VenaSeal is non-thermal, some patients may return to usual activities relatively soon, but recovery time and activity advice vary.

Comparative studies have reported differences in post-procedure pain and bruising between VenaSeal and thermal ablation, but outcomes vary and should be discussed with the treating clinician.

Name: Platelet-Rich Plasma
Main Headline: PRP Treatment in Ahmedabad & Vadodara Gujarat – Bankers Vascular Hospital
Department Short Details: Bankers Vascular Hospital Vadodara & Vadodara Gujarat provides PRP therapy for chronic tendon injuries, muscle pain and joint pain. Non-surgical, natural healing with platelet-rich plasma.
Department Details:
What is PRP in MSK Interventions?

PRP (Platelet-Rich Plasma) is a biologic injection treatment that uses a concentration of a patient’s own platelets. It is used in selected musculoskeletal conditions with the aim of supporting healing and symptom management, although evidence and response vary by condition, such as:

  • Tendons (tendinosis, partial tears)
  • Ligaments (sprains, partial tears)
  • Muscles (chronic strain, myofascial pain)
  • Joints (osteoarthritis, cartilage  damage)
  • Fascia / Enthesis (plantar fasciitis)

Mechanism of Action

  • Platelets release growth factors like   PDGF, VEGF, TGF-β
  • Stimulate:
       
  • Angiogenesis (new blood vessels)
       
  • Collagen synthesis
       
  • Stem cell recruitment
  • Result: tissue repair and regeneration

Procedure (MSK Interventional Approach)

·    Patient Selection & Assessment

o   History,imaging (USG/MRI), physical exam

o   Rule out contraindications (infection, severe anemia, coagulopathy)

·    Blood Collection & PRP Preparation

o   Draw 15–60 ml of blood

o   Centrifuge to get platelet-rich plasma (2–5x platelet concentration)

·   Image-Guided Injection

o   Ultrasound or fluoroscopy guidance ensures precise delivery

o   Inject PRP into target site (tendon, joint, ligament)

·   Post-Procedure Protocol

o   Relative rest for 1–2 days

o   Gradual physiotherapy & rehabilitation

o   Avoid NSAIDs(they block platelet action)

Advantages in MSK Intervention

  • Minimally invasive (day-care procedure)
  • Uses a patient’s own platelet concentrate as part of treatment
  • May be considered as one option before surgery in selected cases
  • Works well with physiotherapy & exercise programs

Limitations

  • Takes time (weeks to months for full effect)
  • May require 1–3 sessions depending on severity
  • Evidence strongest for tendinopathy  and knee OA, less for severe ligament tears
  • Not suitable if patient has active  infection, severe thrombocytopenia, Rheumatoid arthritis, cancer near injection site
